summary: At nearly 13,825 people per square mile packed into just 4.8 square miles, Lynwood is denser than several well-known urban cores in the U.S. — yet it sits on the dead-flat Los Angeles Basin floor with no hills, no vistas, and no topographic drama whatsoever, just a low-slung grid of single-family homes and commercial strips stretching to the horizon. That flatness does mean the climate is remarkably even: annual daytime highs average 76°F with 9.3 hours of sunshine per day, producing a year-round outdoor-comfortable baseline that genuinely differs from hillier, foggier pockets of the LA metro. The city functions largely as a bedroom community; the I-105 freeway bisects it east-to-west and the Metro Green Line cuts through, giving commuters a rail option toward LAX or Norwalk, but the freeway also fragments the street grid and creates abrupt transitions between residential blocks and commercial-industrial stretches. A median home value of $569,400 against a median household income of $70,236 yields a price-to-income ratio above 8:1 — meaning homeownership requires either substantial savings or dual incomes, while the $1,625 median rent consumes roughly 28% of that same median income, landing in a more manageable range. Motor vehicle theft stands out sharply at 1,279 per 100K, one of the higher rates in the region and worth factoring into insurance costs and daily logistics. Lynwood is a place where affordability relative to the broader LA housing market coexists with infrastructure tradeoffs that the numbers make hard to ignore.
